transcript:
This is NPR News now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
Russia launched a massive overnight assault on Ukraine's capital, Kiev.
Russian President Putin is vowing to retaliate for Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch Bridge.
That links the annexed Crimean Peninsula to Russia.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports.
Intermittent waves of ballistic missiles and drones attacked the city throughout the night
as witnessed by NPR.
The hours-long assault disrupted electricity, heating and water supplies, and damaged three
bridges linking the city's left and right banks.
Ukrainian lawmaker Alexander Moresko says for Putin, the Crimea Bridge is an important
symbol of Russian domination of Ukraine.
"And now when it was destroyed, especially on the eve of his meetings with President
Trump and a Chinese leader, it's extremely embarrassing.
It's humiliating for Putin."
Russia says the bridge will be repaired, but experts say given the structural damage, that
will be extremely difficult, especially during a war.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kiev.
The U.S. Army is delaying today's controlled explosion of thousands of pounds of bomb-making
material until Monday.
They want to prevent an accidental blast at the site in southeastern Iowa.
At Iowa Public Radio's Eliza Billingham says, "The blast is expected to create a cloud
of toxic dust, and it is not clear where that could float."
Most Iowans didn't find out that this was happening until the beginning of this week.
And yesterday afternoon, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sued the EPA.
Elected officials started calling for the army to pause its operations and better assess
risks.
And last night, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Tell announced on social media that the
army would delay until Monday, which he called the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted
temperature drop.
Army spokesperson Justine Berrati had said previously that cold weather would make the
situation even more dangerous.
Eliza Billingham reporting, "A new study shows that six in ten people who use artificial
intelligence for health advice say they would believe a chatbot, even if it contradicted
their health care provider."
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports.
Talker Research conducted the survey for the virtual care company MD Live.
Medical director Dr. Maggie Williams says chatbots give quick, confident answers at
any hour.
By the time patients come in, she says, many have already asked a chatbot about their symptoms.
That happens every day, multiple times a day, and I think, honestly, many of our patients
have conferred with clod or another resource and maybe don't even disclose it.
Williams says the risk goes both ways.
A chatbot could get someone to the ER sooner, but it can also suggest breathing exercises
for chest pressure when someone's having a heart attack.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
This is NPR.
The incoming chair of the House Judiciary Committee in the next Congress is investigating
how Homeland Security and Justice Department officials preserve communications when they're
doing official business.
Maryland Democratic Congressman Jamie Raskin has sent letters warning that he is concerned
the Trump administration is using apps that self-delete after a certain period of time.
Raskin says that would violate laws about governmental record keeping.
He is demanding that the agencies take steps to recover any deletions.
Storms, driven by the weather pattern known as El Nino, have been slamming California
this week.
It's caused flooding in cities, including San Francisco.
From member station KQED, Ezra David Romero reports, streets have turned into rivers and
cars floated in the floodwaters.
San Francisco's mostly flat mission district was hit hard by the rain on Wednesday.
Rich Deliah armored his bagel shop, Bagledo, with a metal flood wall.
But water still spilled out of every drain and toilet in his shop.
He says it ruined the rebuild he completed just a few years back.
We have machines, mixers, ovens, obviously with the water there we didn't really want
to plug anything in and see if it worked.
While he's nervous about a storm this weekend and a potential atmospheric river next week,
he's even more worried about how El Nino could cause a wetter than average winter for California.
For NPR News, I'm Ezra David Romero in San Francisco.

topics.text: Russia launches massive overnight assault on Kyiv, disrupting power, heat, and water supplies
Army delays controlled explosion of bomb-making material at southeastern Iowa site until Monday
Survey finds six in ten AI health-advice users would trust a chatbot over their provider
Rep. Jamie Raskin demands agencies recover messages from self-deleting apps used by DHS and DOJ
El Niño-driven storms cause flooding across California, including San Francisco's Mission district
